extracted.intended_audience: employers, occupational safety and health professionals, workplace compliance officers, and stakeholders submitting comments on the OSHA heat-illness NPRM
extracted.subtask_description: Extraction of proposed OSHA regulatory requirements and evaluative criteria for preventing heat-related illness in workplaces, including acclimatization, rest breaks, communication, PPE maintenance, and high-heat protections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exception to acclimatization for new/returning employees (same or similar conditions)
rubrics_metrics.description: The employee must have engaged in similar work activities in the similar heat conditions consistently over the preceding 14 days for the exception to apply.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA intends “consistently” to mean the employee engaged in the task for at least two hours per day on a majority of the preceding 14 days. Examples when the exception would not apply: prior positions ended longer than 14 days ago; prior positions ended within last 14 days but were in cooler conditions; prior positions ended within last 14 days but were hotter with less exertion; prior positions ended less than 14 days ago but the employee did not perform similar tasks in similar heat for at least two hours per day on a majority of the preceding 14 days. To demonstrate compliance, employers could obtain information directly from the new employee (verbally or in writing) about timing, location, duration, and type of prior work. Asking only “did you consistently work under the same or similar conditions” without supporting details is not sufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Employer verification of prior acclimatization status
rubrics_metrics.description: To demonstrate that a new employee consistently worked under the same or similar conditions within the prior 14 days, the employer must obtain supporting details from the employee.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employer could ask questions verbally or in writing about prior work (timing, location, duration, type of work). If employer only asks a yes/no question without supporting details, the requirement would not be satisfied. OSHA is concerned about incentives for employees to lie or employer pressure to misreport; seeks comments on likelihood and mitigation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acclimatization program requirements/options (general)
rubrics_metrics.description: OSHA proposes acclimatization requirements/options (including following high heat trigger requirements or a gradual increase in exposure option) and seeks comment on various acclimatization elements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Questions for stakeholders include whether the term “same or similar conditions” is sufficiently clear; whether a minimum amount of heat exposure to achieve acclimatization should be specified under a gradual-acclimatization option; whether acclimatization protocols should be required during local heat waves and how to define heat waves; whether annual acclimatization at the beginning of each heat season should be required and how to implement it; examples of protocols for industries where new hires cannot do heat-exposed tasks in week one; additional requirements for employees returning after <14 days with acute illnesses (fever, GI infections); and whether additional requirements are needed for employees starting/returning when heat index is above 90°F (e.g., more frequent/longer breaks).

rubrics_metrics.name: Allow and encourage rest breaks if needed to prevent overheating (paragraph e(8))
rubrics_metrics.description: Employers must allow and encourage employees to take paid rest breaks in required break areas if needed to prevent overheating.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rest breaks allow employees to reduce work rate, hydrate, cool down (shade, air-conditioned, or cooled areas), remove PPE contributing to heat strain. Employees may decide timing/frequency; unscheduled breaks must be heat-related (only if needed to prevent overheating). If leaving a workstation would create hazard or harm equipment/product, employer may require notification and relief by a supervisor who is immediately available. Employers should periodically remind employees of the option to take rest breaks. Employer may also ask or direct an employee to take a rest break if signs of excessive heat strain are observed. Slowing work pace or performing sedentary activity is not a rest break. Rest breaks must be taken in break areas required under paragraphs (e)(3) or (4).

rubrics_metrics.name: Paid rest breaks requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Rest breaks taken to prevent overheating must be paid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA preliminarily finds breaks should be paid so employees are not discouraged from taking them. This includes both mandatory breaks and breaks needed to prevent overheating. Employers should ensure compensation approaches (including for piece-rate workers) so employees are not financially penalized for taking these breaks. OSHA references Explanation of Proposed Requirements for paragraph (j) for how to ensure breaks are implemented at no cost to employees.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characteristics and limits of unscheduled rest breaks
rubrics_metrics.description: Unscheduled rest breaks typically last less than 15 minutes; breaks that extend beyond 15 minutes or frequent unscheduled breaks may indicate an HRI.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of signs prompting a rest break include excessive thirst, excessive sweating, general feeling of unwellness attributed to heat, or difficulty performing a task they normally can. Rest breaks do not need to be tied to symptoms. If a rest break extends beyond 15 minutes or occurs very frequently, employer should consider whether the employee is experiencing HRI and follow the relieving-from-duty requirements in paragraph (g)(2).

rubrics_metrics.name: Effective two-way regular communication (paragraph e(9))
rubrics_metrics.description: Employers must maintain effective, two-way communication with employees and regularly communicate with employees at the initial heat trigger.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Means of communication must be effective (voice/hand signals may suffice when employees are nearby; otherwise electronic means like handheld transceivers, phone, or radio may be needed). If using electronic means, employer must respond in a timely manner (a phone number with no timely response is not effective). Communication must be two-way so employees can report signs/symptoms and employers can notify employees. Employers must ensure regular contact (e.g., every few hours) either by employer outreach or a system requiring employee check-ins; if employees must initiate contact, employer must reach out within a reasonable time if no response. The requirement also applies to employees who work alone, though methods may differ. OSHA requests comments on typical intervals and challenges for communicating with lone workers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain cooling properties of cooling PPE (paragraph e(10))
rubrics_metrics.description: If employers provide cooling PPE (e.g., cooling vests), they must ensure the PPE's cooling properties are maintained at all times during use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The standard does not require employers to provide cooling PPE, but provided cooling PPE must be maintained because loss of cooling properties (e.g., melted ice packs) can increase heat retention and risk of HRI. OSHA requests comments on scenarios where wearing cooling PPE is warranted and feasible and whether OSHA should require its use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing of protections when high heat trigger met (paragraph f)
rubrics_metrics.description: When employees are exposed at or above the high heat trigger (heat index of 90°F or corresponding WBGT), employers must provide the protections in paragraph (f) during the time employees are exposed at or above the high heat trigger; protections in paragraph (e) remain in effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employer obligations apply only during periods of exposure at/above the trigger (e.g., if heat index rises mid-shift, protections apply for that portion). The high heat trigger is described as heat index 90°F or a corresponding WBGT equal to the NIOSH REL. Protections in paragraphs (f)(2)–(f)(5) are in addition to requirements at the initial heat trigger (paragraph e).

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimum mandatory rest breaks at or above high heat trigger (paragraph f(2))
rubrics_metrics.description: When the high heat trigger is met or exceeded, employers must provide a minimum 15-minute paid rest break at least every two hours in required break areas; these breaks are mandatory and the employer must ensure they are taken.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This minimum (15 minutes every 2 hours) is derived as highly protective and administratively convenient. The requirement is additive to paragraph (e)(8) (allowing/encouraging unscheduled breaks); if an employee takes a 15-minute break under (e)(8), it affects when the next mandatory (f)(2) break is due. Meal breaks that are bona fide and not required to be paid under law may count as a rest break (employee must be completely relieved of duties). Time to put on/remove PPE and time to walk to/from break area are excluded from the 15-minute rest break. Rest breaks are not satisfied by slowing the pace of work or by performing sedentary work in a break area. Employers may provide longer/more frequent breaks and may use strategies to accommodate operational needs (staggering breaks, portable shade, scheduling cooler work times). OSHA acknowledges some employer implementation challenges and requests comment.
